summary: This document defines security requirements for time protocols, focusing on PTP and NTP. It also discusses the security impact of time protocol practices and the performance implications of security mechanisms.

eli5.summary: Clocks in computers need to agree, and bad guys might trick them. This RFC lists what must be done to keep time-sharing protocols safe from tampering.

subtitle: What a security scheme for NTP and PTP must do, so that a forged or delayed clock cannot quietly corrupt network time.

tldr.problem: Time protocols such as NTP and PTP are widely deployed, yet an attacker who compromises one can feed false time to every application that depends on it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes the attacks (spoofing, replay, rogue masters, delay manipulation and more) and turns them into MUST, SHOULD and MAY requirements for any security mechanism, without defining the mechanism itself.
tldr.outcome: Vendors, standards bodies and operators get a checklist to design or judge time-protocol security, and a warning that security and clock accuracy pull in different directions.

facts.label: Secure mode
facts.value: MUST discard packets from unsecured clocks

today: RFC 7384 is an Informational document published in October 2014, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines requirements rather than a protocol, and it states that security solutions that meet them are outside its scope.

sections.title: Why Time Protocols Need Security
sections.content:
RFC 7384 looks at the security of time distribution protocols in packet networks, focusing on the Network Time Protocol (NTP) and the Precision Time Protocol (PTP). PTP was not defined by the IETF, but it is included because it is one of the two most common time protocols.

NTP already has security built in: NTPv4 uses a symmetric key scheme and Autokey (RFC 5906) uses public keys. PTP's experimental security protocol in Annex K of IEEE 1588 was never formalized into a fully defined protocol. The RFC says this gap undoubtedly contributed to the wide deployment of unsecured time synchronization.

The document is aimed at equipment vendors, standards bodies and network operators. It also says that security is not always strictly necessary: the benefits must be weighed against the risks for each specific system.
sections.eli5: Two common ways to share the time over a network are NTP and PTP. One came with a lock and the other mostly did not, so this document says what a good lock should look like.

sections.title: Common Vocabulary for PTP and NTP
sections.content:
To talk about both protocols at once, the RFC uses one set of words. A master is a PTP master or an NTP server, and a slave is a PTP slave or an NTP client. A grandmaster gets its time from a locally attached clock device, not through the network. An intermediate clock receives time from a master and passes it on: in NTP an intermediate clock is a server that is not Stratum 1, and in PTP it is a Boundary Clock (BC) or Transparent Clock (TC).

Two security styles matter later. In end-to-end security, intermediate nodes do not modify secured packets. In hop-by-hop security, intermediate nodes share the key and may modify and re-protect packets. A secured clock meets the requirements of this document; an unsecured clock does not.
sections.eli5: The document gives both protocols the same names for the same jobs: a master is whoever tells the time, and a slave is whoever listens. That way one set of rules can cover both.

sections.title: The Threat Model and Attacks
sections.content:
Attackers are sorted two ways. Internal attackers hold keys or sit in a trusted part of the network; external attackers see only protected traffic. A man in the middle (MITM) can intercept and modify packets in flight, while a packet injector can only generate packets, though it may record multicast packets and replay them later.

The threat analysis lists twelve attacks, among them:

  • Packet manipulation: an MITM alters packets so the protocol looks healthy but gives wrong time.
  • Spoofing: an injector pretends to be a master, or a slave, so the victim computes delays from false information.
  • Replay: recorded packets are sent again later.
  • Rogue master: the attacker does not fake an identity but manipulates master election, for example the PTP Best Master Clock Algorithm (BMCA).
  • Delay manipulation: an MITM adds a constant, jittered or slowly wandering delay to packets.
  • Cryptographic performance attacks: fake packets force the receiver to burn effort verifying them.
  • Time source attacks, such as jamming or faking a GPS signal, which the RFC treats as outside the scope of the time protocol.

The RFC also lists interception and removal, L2/L3 denial of service, DoS against the time protocol, exploiting protocol vulnerabilities, and network reconnaissance. Its summary table shows that external attackers have far less impact once authentication and integrity protection are in place.
sections.eli5: A sneaky person might copy a time announcement, change it, replay an old one, pretend to be the boss clock, or slow the messages down. Each trick makes your clock wrong in a different way.

sections.title: The Security Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC does not define a security mechanism. It states what any mechanism should do, in the form "the security mechanism MUST/SHOULD/MAY ...". Some requirements could be met with existing tools such as IPsec or MACsec. The level of each requirement depends on its impact, how hard the matching attack is, and practical considerations.

The MUST requirements are:

  • Authentication and authorization, including slaves checking that a master is allowed to be a master, and recursive checking through intermediate clocks (a chain of trust).
  • In PTP, authentication of Announce and Management messages.
  • Protection of packet integrity, spoofing prevention, and replay protection.
  • Key refresh, and no significant loss in time quality from the security mechanism.
  • Protection against MITM attacks that degrade clock accuracy, for example with redundant masters or redundant paths.
  • A secure mode in which packets from unsecured clocks are discarded.

The SHOULD items cover DoS mitigation, security association protocols for unicast and multicast, low computation, storage and bandwidth overhead, and a hybrid mode. The MAY items cover a master authenticating its slaves (it can cost the server more than serving an unauthorized client), authenticating P2P Transparent Clocks, PTP Signaling messages, and confidentiality, since timing information is usually not secret.
sections.eli5: The rules say who must prove who they are, that messages must not be changed or replayed, and that keys must be swapped often. Some rules are strict, some are advice, and some are optional extras.

sections.title: Secured and Unsecured Clocks Together
sections.content:
Adding security is complex and expensive, so networks may need to deploy it step by step. The RFC requires a secure mode, where only secured clocks take part. It recommends (SHOULD) a hybrid mode, where secured and unsecured clocks mix, as a way to migrate gradually. In hybrid mode a master SHOULD be a secured clock and a secured slave SHOULD discard packets from unsecured clocks.

The RFC points out that NTPv4 with Autokey does not meet this: a Stratum 2 server connected to Server A (with authentication) and Server B (without) will choose B if B has the more accurate clock.
sections.eli5: When only some clocks have a lock, the safe ones should listen only to other locked clocks. The best plan is for every clock to get a lock.

sections.title: Side Effects and Dependencies
sections.content:
The RFC also looks at how security and time interact. Timestamps are often added as a packet is sent, so encryption or integrity protection MUST be applied after the timestamp is inserted. A security engine sitting between the timestamping function and the wire can add non-deterministic latency and hurt accuracy. PTP's two-step mode avoids modifying packets, but IPsec can make time packets impossible to identify.

Intermediate clocks create a trade-off. High accuracy calls for on-path, hop-by-hop help; robust security calls for end-to-end protection. In PTP's end-to-end approach the correctionField that Transparent Clocks update needs its own protection, which is harder to implement. Hop-by-hop is simpler but lets rogue TCs modify packets.

Finally, time and security depend on each other. Certificate validation needs roughly synchronized clocks, so IKEv2, TLS and Kerberos all rely on time, while Autokey needs a valid certificate to trust time. An attack that sets clocks back could let an expired key be used again. Key distribution is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Locks and clocks need each other: you need the right time to check a lock, and you need a lock to trust the time. Adding more guards on the path can also make the message arrive a little later.
